format: Each lesson has five formative questions (error, guided1, guided2, independent1, independent2) then two distinct required-check questions. Each row is prompt, correct option, distractors, explanatory feedback.

13: A learner says a gene, DNA and a chromosome are exactly the same object. What is the correction?
A gene is a DNA region; chromosomes package long DNA molecules containing many genes.
A visible chromosome shape directly reveals every gene on that chromosome.
Chromosomes contain no DNA.
The three names refer to related but different scales of organization.
What letters pair across the rungs of A-G-C-T-G?
T-C-G-A-C.
A-G-C-T-G.
G-A-T-C-A.
A pairs with T and C with G at each aligned position.
A karyotype shows three copies of chromosome 21. What pattern is visible?
Trisomy 21.
A one-letter DNA substitution.
Proof of every future health outcome.
The image can show a chromosome-number difference at the labelled pair.
A student uses XX/XY as a universal rule for a person's gender. What is the problem?
They are common chromosome patterns with variations and do not establish gender identity.
Chromosomes cannot be observed.
Every human body cell contains one unpaired chromosome.
Genomic variation and personal identity exceed a simplified classroom karyotype model.
Which claim is beyond what a karyotype image alone can show?
A karyotype reveals every small sequence variant and predicts a precise lifetime outcome.
The number of visible chromosome 21 copies.
Whether a labelled pair appears in the display.
Karyotypes show large patterns, not all sequence-level or future information.
Which evidence would support calling a pattern XXY in a source karyotype?
Two X chromosomes and one Y chromosome visibly grouped as sex chromosomes.
Three copies of chromosome 21.
A person reporting a cough.
The label follows the observed chromosome set, not a personal diagnosis or unrelated symptom.
A page says 'normal human has 46 chromosomes.' How should the course frame it?
Most body cells typically have 46; variations exist and require careful interpretation.
Every cell in every human always has 46.
Chromosome count alone describes a person's worth.
Typical count is a useful reference, not a universal claim about all cells or people.
14: A learner says a four-box Punnett square promises four children with one outcome each. What is the error?
Boxes show possible allele combinations and probabilities, not guaranteed family outcomes.
The four boxes record four children who have already been born.
Each child must use a different box.
Each offspring is another possible outcome under the model.
What gametes can a Tt plant contribute in the simple model?
T or t.
Only TT.
Only tt.
A gamete receives one allele for the modeled gene.
What genotype ratio comes from Ww × Ww?
1 WW : 2 Ww : 1 ww.
4 WW : 0 Ww : 0 ww.
1 WW : 1 ww with no heterozygotes.
Combining W and w from each parent gives WW, Ww, Ww and ww.
If white wool is dominant to black, what phenotype ratio does Ww × Ww predict?
3 white : 1 black in the simplified model.
1 white : 3 black.
Four black lambs guaranteed.
Three of four equally likely boxes have at least one dominant W allele.
Why must the workbook's brown/blue human-eye-colour square have a caution note?
Real eye colour involves multiple genes; the one-gene rule is a classroom simplification.
One allele pair is enough to predict every detail of human eye colour.
The four boxes guarantee four specific children.
The model teaches allele bookkeeping but not a reliable personal eye-colour forecast.
A Tt plant is crossed with tt. Which prediction is correct?
Half Tt tall and half tt short under the model.
All TT tall.
All tt short.
Tt contributes T or t and tt contributes t, producing a 1:1 split.
Two white Ww sheep have two white lambs. Does this disprove a 3:1 prediction?
No; a small family may differ from the long-run probability.
Yes; the square guarantees one black in every four births.
Yes; all offspring must be WW.
Probabilities describe independent chances, not exact short sequences.
15: A learner uses the named-family pedigree from workbook p. 31 to answer Q12 on p. 32. What is the error?
Q12 has its own pedigree on p. 32, so its inheritance claim must be tested against that figure.
The family names on p. 31 automatically apply to every later pedigree.
Shading has the same meaning as a person’s name.
Q11 and Q12 use different pedigrees. Evidence from the named-family chart on p. 31 cannot replace the separate Q12 chart on p. 32.
How many generations appear on workbook p. 31?
Three.
Two, because only two shaded people appear.
Four, because four names are shaded.
Generation count follows horizontal descent levels, not affected count.
Which named people are shaded in the source pedigree?
Sue, Joe, Jim and Tim.
Tom, Sara, Kay and Lori.
Only Sue and Kay.
The page key defines shading as affected status; read each named symbol.
How many children does Jim have in the drawn family?
Two: Tim and Lori.
Four: Sue, Joe, Tim and Lori.
One: Kay.
Follow Jim and Kay's parent line to their two descendants.
Which feature of the separate Q12 pedigree supports a recessive interpretation in the intended simple model?
Two parents who do not display the trait have a child who does display it.
Every person in the pedigree displays the trait.
The chart prints every person’s genotype.
The Q12 chart includes two unshaded parents with a shaded child. In the intended fully penetrant dominant-or-recessive classroom model, both parents can be unaffected carriers of a recessive allele.
The original wording calls shaded people 'infected' and then asks for inherited pattern. What should online instruction do?
Preserve the source wording but explain shading as an affected trait status for this genetics model.
Teach ordinary infection as a simple allele automatically inherited by children.
Delete the diagram so the inconsistency cannot be seen.
The source is visible, while the authored science distinguishes infection from inherited traits.
What must a constructed pedigree include to make its symbols interpretable?
A key for symbols and shading, generation structure and the stated relationships.
Names alone, without symbols or relationship lines, are enough to show inheritance.
A claim that eye colour is always one-gene in real people.
A keyed diagram shows observations and relationships; the workbook's eye-colour rule remains a limited model.
16: A learner says every mutation is harmful and inherited. What is the correction?
Effects vary, and a body-cell change is not automatically passed to children.
Every mutation produces an obvious beneficial trait.
Every DNA difference is visible on a karyotype.
Location, effect and cell lineage matter before claiming harm or inheritance.
What makes a body-cell change different from one in a reproductive-cell lineage?
Only a change in reproductive cells normally has a direct route to offspring.
Body cells contain no DNA.
A reproductive cell cannot contain variants.
Inheritance requires a route through egg or sperm formation.
A base is copied differently and repair corrects it. What follows?
The copying error need not persist as a new variant in that lineage.
A genetic disorder is guaranteed.
Every DNA copying error changes the total chromosome count.
Repair can prevent a transient copying error from becoming a lasting sequence change.
Why can't exposure to a mutagen prove a specific future disorder?
Exposure may raise risk, but dose, repair, location and chance affect outcomes.
Mutagens have no possible effects.
A given exposure always causes the same mutation and outcome in every person.
Risk is probabilistic and mechanism-specific, not an individual guarantee.
Which statement about amniocentesis is appropriate for this course?
It involves possible information, procedure risks and personal decisions needing clinical counselling.
The class should choose it for each pregnant person.
It guarantees the child's whole future.
The course can analyze evidence and ethics without making an individual medical decision.
A DNA change lies outside a protein-coding sequence. Which conclusion is justified?
Its effect still depends on location and function; it cannot be assumed harmful or harmless from that fact alone.
Every non-coding change is harmless.
Every non-coding change is lethal.
Regulatory regions and other contexts can matter, and evidence is needed.
Which chain is most careful when explaining a possible genetic disorder?
Describe the change, cell lineage and functional effect, then the evidence linking it to the condition.
Name one exposure and guarantee a named disorder.
Assume all inherited variants cause illness.
A causal explanation needs more than the word mutation.
17: A headline says a genetic test proves someone will develop a complex disease. What is missing?
Predictive strength, other genes, environment, age and uncertainty.
More precise-looking chart colours without stronger evidence.
A claim that genetic results can never inform any health decision.
Genetic association or screening result is not always a certain personal forecast.
What makes consent meaningful in a genetic study?
Understanding purpose, data use, risks and alternatives before a voluntary decision.
A signature obtained without explanation.
A decision based on a headline without checking the original evidence.
Informed consent includes comprehension and choice about the proposed use.
Why can genetic privacy matter to relatives?
Shared inherited information may imply something about family members too.
Relatives have identical genetic information whenever they share a pedigree.
Genetic data are never personal.
Family relationships make some genetic findings relevant beyond one data record.
The workbook asks about cloning someone to harvest organs. Which response is ethical reasoning?
Assess claimed benefit, harm, consent, dignity, fairness and alternatives rather than treating a person as a resource.
Assume the hypothetical is standard clinical practice.
Use an unsupported slogan rather than evidence about benefits and harms.
A justified response separates a technology claim from the rights of affected people.
A dated chart calls an idea an 'advance'. What should be checked?
Its date, evidence, current status, limits and who benefits or bears risk.
A professional-looking logo is enough to establish the chart’s evidence.
Whether the old prediction sounds exciting.
Research examples change; source context and present evidence must be kept separate.
What can a genetic screen establish most directly?
The specified pattern it measured, interpreted within its accuracy and context.
Every future symptom and life choice.
A person's worth or full identity.
A screen measures defined genetic information; interpretation may require more evidence.
Which four-part question set best evaluates a new genetic technology?
Benefit evidence, harms/uncertainty, consent/privacy, and fair access or alternatives.
Only speed, marketing, colour and novelty.
Only whether the technology is possible.
Scientific value and ethical acceptability require several linked kinds of evidence.
